claim: Spermatogonial cells (SPGs) are undifferentiated male germ cells in testis that are quiescent until birth.
source: In mammals, spermatogonial cells (SPGs) are undifferentiated male germ cells in testis that are quiescent until birth and then self-renew and differentiate to produce spermatogenic cells and functional sperm from early postnatal life throughout adulthood.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the biological characteristics of SPGs, drawing on established scientific knowledge about mammalian germ cell biology.

claim: SPGs self-renew and differentiate to produce spermatogenic cells and functional sperm from early postnatal life throughout adulthood.
source: In mammals, spermatogonial cells (SPGs) are undifferentiated male germ cells in testis that are quiescent until birth and then self-renew and differentiate to produce spermatogenic cells and functional sperm from early postnatal life throughout adulthood.
evidence: This statement describes the known biological function of SPGs based on established scientific understanding.

claim: The transcriptome of SPGs is highly dynamic and timely regulated during postnatal development.
source: The transcriptome of SPGs is highly dynamic and timely regulated during postnatal development.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's own RNA-seq data and references to prior literature on SPG transcriptomics.

claim: SPGs undergo massive chromatin remodeling during postnatal development.
source: By integrating transcriptomic and epigenomic features, we show that SPGs undergo massive chromatin remodeling during postnatal development that partially correlates with distinct gene expression profiles and transcription factors (TF) motif enrichment.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the ATAC-seq data presented in the study showing differentially accessible regions.

claim: Chromatin remodeling in SPGs during postnatal development partially correlates with distinct gene expression profiles.
source: By integrating transcriptomic and epigenomic features, we show that SPGs undergo massive chromatin remodeling during postnatal development that partially correlates with distinct gene expression profiles and transcription factors (TF) motif enrichment.
evidence: This is based on the integrated analysis of RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data showing some but not complete correspondence between transcriptional changes and chromatin accessibility.

claim: Genomic regions with significantly different chromatin accessibility in adult SPGs are marked by histone modifications associated with enhancers and promoters.
source: We identify genomic regions with significantly different chromatin accessibility in adult SPGs that are marked by histone modifications associated with enhancers and promoters.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of ATAC-seq data with publicly available ChIP-seq data for histone modifications.

claim: Some regions with increased accessibility correspond to transposable element subtypes enriched in multiple TFs motifs and close to differentially expressed genes.
source: Some of the regions with increased accessibility correspond to transposable element subtypes enriched in multiple TFs motifs and close to differentially expressed genes.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of TEs in ATAC-seq data combined with motif enrichment and proximity to DEGs.

claim: In the mammalian testis, primordial germ cells (PGCs) give rise sequentially to different populations of SPGs: primary transitional (T1)-prospermatogonia (ProSG), secondary transitional (T2)-ProSG and then spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs).
source: In the mammalian testis, the founding germ cells are primordial germ cells (PGCs), which give rise sequentially to different populations of SPGs: primary transitional (T1)-prospermatogonia (ProSG), secondary transitional (T2)-ProSG and then spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) (McCarrey, 2013; Rabbani et al., 2022; Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on germ cell development.

claim: The ProSG population is exhausted by postnatal day (PND) 5.
source: The ProSG population is exhausted by postnatal day (PND) 5 (Drumond et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Drumond et al., 2011.

claim: By PND6-8, distinct SPGs subtypes can be distinguished on the basis of specific marker proteins and regenerative capacity.
source: by PND6-8, distinct SPGs subtypes can be distinguished on the basis of specific marker proteins and regenerative capacity (Cheng et al., 2020; Ernst et al., 2019; Green et al., 2018; Hermann et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies characterizing SPG subtypes.

claim: SSCs represent an undifferentiated population of SPGs that retain regenerative capacity and divide to either self-renew or generate progenitors that initiate spermatogenic differentiation.
source: SSCs represent an undifferentiated population of SPGs that retain regenerative capacity and divide to either self-renew or generate progenitors that initiate spermatogenic differentiation, giving rise to differentiating SPGs (diff-SPGs).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of SSC biology.

claim: Diff-SPGs form chains of daughter cells that become primary and secondary spermatocytes around PND10 to 12.
source: Diff-SPGs form chains of daughter cells that become primary and secondary spermatocytes around PND10 to 12.
evidence: This describes the known developmental timeline of spermatogenesis.

claim: Spermatocytes undergo meiosis and give rise to haploid spermatids that develop into spermatozoa.
source: Spermatocytes then undergo meiosis and give rise to haploid spermatids that develop into spermatozoa.
evidence: This describes the established process of spermatogenesis.

claim: Spermatozoa are released into the lumen of seminiferous tubules and continue to mature in the epididymis until becoming capable of fertilization by PND42-48 in mice.
source: Spermatozoa are then released into the lumen of seminiferous tubules and continue to mature in the epididymis until becoming capable of fertilization by PND42-48 in mice (de Rooij, 2017; Kubota and Brinster, 2018; Oatley and Griswold, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on sperm maturation in mice.

claim: SPGs in early postnatal life have distinct transcriptional signatures.
source: Recent work showed that SPGs in early postnatal life have distinct transcriptional signatures (Green et al., 2018; Hammoud et al., 2014; Hermann et al., 2018; Law et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies characterizing SPG transcriptomes.

claim: During the first week of postnatal development, SPGs display unique features necessary for the rapid establishment and expansion of the cell population along the basement membrane.
source: During the first week of postnatal development, SPGs display unique features necessary for the rapid establishment and expansion of the cell population along the basement membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biological function of early postnatal SPGs.

claim: Early postnatal SPGs have high expression of genes involved in cell cycle regulation, stem cell proliferation, transcription, and RNA processing.
source: This includes high expression of genes involved in cell cycle regulation, stem cell proliferation, transcription, and RNA processing (Grive et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grive et al., 2019.

claim: Genes expressed in adult SPGs are involved in the maintenance of a balance between proliferation and differentiation.
source: In comparison, genes expressed in adult SPGs are involved in the maintenance of a balance between proliferation and differentiation and help constitute a steady cell population that ensures sperm formation across life.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of genes expressed in adult SPGs.

claim: Adult SPGs prioritize pathways related to paracrine signaling and niche communication, as well as mitochondrial functions and oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Previous transcriptome analyses have revealed that adult SPGs prioritize pathways related to paracrine signaling and niche communication, as well as mitochondrial functions and oxidative phosphorylation (Grive et al., 2019; Hermann et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous transcriptome studies.

claim: Changes to chromatin accessibility, histone tail modifications and DNA methylation have been reported in SPGs during postnatal development.
source: In addition, changes to chromatin accessibility, histone tail modifications and DNA methylation have also been reported in SPGs during postnatal development (Maezawa et al., 2018; Hammoud et al., 2014; Hammoud et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on epigenetic changes in SPGs.

claim: The relationship between transcriptome dynamics and chromatin landscape in SPGs during the transition from early postnatal to adult stage has not been fully characterized.
source: Today however, the relationship between transcriptome dynamics and chromatin landscape in SPGs during the transition from early postnatal to adult stage has not been fully characterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: FACS enriched cell populations from 3–6% PLZF + (before FACS) to 85–95% PLZF+.
source: FACS enriched cell populations from 3–6% PLZF + (before FACS) to 85–95% PLZF+ (Figure 1B), suggesting high SPGs enrichment.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Classical SPGs markers such as Kit, Id4, Lin28a, Zbtb16, and Gfra1 were robustly expressed in all SPGs samples at each developmental stage.
source: Classical SPGs markers such as Kit (Schrans-Stassen et al., 1999), Id4 (Helsel et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2015), Lin28a (Chakraborty et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020), Zbtb16 (Costoya et al., 2004; Song et al., 2020), and Gfra1 (He et al., 2007) were robustly expressed in all SPGs samples at each developmental stage (Figure 1C), indicating high purity of sorted cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and citations to studies identifying these markers.

claim: Low to negligible expression of somatic cells markers such as Vim and Tspan17 for Sertoli cells, and Fabp3 and Hsd3b1 for Leydig cells was detected.
source: In contrast, low to negligible expression of somatic cells markers such as Vim (Bernardino et al., 2018) and Tspan17 (Gewiss et al., 2021) for Sertoli cells, and Fabp3 and Hsd3b1 for Leydig cells (Sararols et al., 2021; Figure 1C) was detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and citations to studies identifying these markers.

claim: Evaluation of postnatal libraries (PND8 and PND15) against a PND6 signature matrix revealed a predominant derivation from SPGs, with average estimated proportions of SSCs being 0.99 and 0.85 for PND8 and PND15 samples, respectively.
source: Evaluation of our postnatal libraries (PND8 and PND15) against a PND6 signature matrix revealed a predominant derivation from SPGs, with average estimated proportions of SSCs being 0.99 and 0.85 for PND8 and PND15 samples, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by deconvolution analysis results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Evaluation of adult RNA-seq libraries using an adult signature matrix showed an average SSCs proportion of 0.82.
source: Similarly, evaluation of our adult RNA-seq libraries using an adult signature matrix, showed an average SSCs proportion of 0.82, indicating a primary derivation from SSCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by deconvolution analysis results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G.

claim: A total of 663 DEGs were identified between PND8 and PND15 (146 down-regulated and 517 up-regulated).
source: A total of 663 DEGs were identified between PND8 and PND15 (146 down-regulated and 517 up-regulated) and 2483 DEGs between PND15 and adult stage (914 down-regulated and 1579 up-regulated) (Figure 1D–E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the differential expression analysis results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 2483 DEGs were identified between PND15 and adult stage (914 down-regulated and 1579 up-regulated).
source: A total of 663 DEGs were identified between PND8 and PND15 (146 down-regulated and 517 up-regulated) and 2483 DEGs between PND15 and adult stage (914 down-regulated and 1579 up-regulated) (Figure 1D–E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the differential expression analysis results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Pou5f1 (Oct4), a TF necessary for pluripotency, is significantly down-regulated in adult SPGs.
source: For instance, Pou5f1 (Oct4), a TF necessary for pluripotency (Nichols et al., 1998), is significantly down-regulated in adult SPGs while the TFs Klf4 and Sox2, also needed for pluripotency (An et al., 2019), are expressed similarly in postnatal and adult stages although at different level (i.e. Klf4 is expressed more than Sox2; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citations to studies on pluripotency factors.

claim: DEGs between PND8 and PND15 are involved in cell differentiation, cilium movement, sperm motility and transcription.
source: GO analyses showed that DEGs between PND8 and PN15 are involved in cell differentiation, cilium movement, sperm motility and transcription and include for instance, TFs such as Junb, Hoxb6, Cebpa, and Pparg (Figure 1F and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis results shown in Figure 1F.

claim: DEGs between PND15 and adulthood play roles in reproduction, spermatogenesis, cell differentiation, DNA replication, glycolysis and extracellular matrix (ECM)-receptor interaction pathways.
source: Further, DEGs between PND15 and adulthood play roles in reproduction, spermatogenesis, cell differentiation, DNA replication, glycolysis and extracellular matrix (ECM)-receptor interaction pathways (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis results shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The DNA methyltransferase Dnmt1, necessary for epi/genome regulation, is specifically down-regulated in adult SPGs.
source: For example, the DNA methyltransferase Dnmt1, necessary for epi/genome regulation (Edwards et al., 2017) and Col4a2, a subunit of type IV collagen and component of the basal membrane (Reissig et al., 2019), are specifically down-regulated in adult SPGs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and a citation to Edwards et al., 2017.

claim: Col4a2, a subunit of type IV collagen and component of the basal membrane, is specifically down-regulated in adult SPGs.
source: For example, the DNA methyltransferase Dnmt1, necessary for epi/genome regulation (Edwards et al., 2017) and Col4a2, a subunit of type IV collagen and component of the basal membrane (Reissig et al., 2019), are specifically down-regulated in adult SPGs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and a citation to Reissig et al., 2019.

claim: Expression of collagen has been associated to a high proliferative potential and the ability to form germ cell colonies in SPGs.
source: Interestingly, expression of collagen has been associated to a high proliferative potential and the ability to form germ cell colonies in SPGs (He et al., 2005), suggesting that regulation of collagen genes in adult SPGs may decrease germ-stem cell potential.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to He et al., 2005.

claim: Regulation of collagen genes in adult SPGs may decrease germ-stem cell potential.
source: Interestingly, expression of collagen has been associated to a high proliferative potential and the ability to form germ cell colonies in SPGs (He et al., 2005), suggesting that regulation of collagen genes in adult SPGs may decrease germ-stem cell potential.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed downregulation of collagen genes and their known function.

claim: 75% (495/663) of DEGs between PND8 and PND15 are not statistically changed in the transition to adult SPGs.
source: For instance, 75% (495/663) of DEGs between PND8 and PND15 are not statistically changed in the transition to adult SPGs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, and Supplementary file 1-Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 93% (2325/2493) of DEGs in adult SPGs are not statistically changed when compared to PND8 versus PND15 SPGs.
source: Similarly, 93% (2325/2493) of DEGs in adult SPGs are not statistically changed when compared to PND8 versus PND15 SPGs (Figure 1H, and Supplementary file 1-Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 4.9% of all DEGs are detected as significantly changed in the same direction and magnitude across the three developmental stages.
source: Interestingly, a small fraction of all DEGs (4.9%) are detected as significantly changed in the same direction and magnitude (adjusted-p ≤0.05, absLog2FC ≥1) across the three developmental stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, and Supplementary file 1-Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: 121 genes are consistently up-regulated from PND8 to adult stage.
source: For instance, 121 genes are consistently up-regulated from PND8 to adult stage, while just 26 are consistently down-regulated from PND8 to adult stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: 26 genes are consistently down-regulated from PND8 to adult stage.
source: For instance, 121 genes are consistently up-regulated from PND8 to adult stage, while just 26 are consistently down-regulated from PND8 to adult stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The histone gene clusters displayed significant down-regulation across postnatal development and in adulthood.
source: In particular, the histone gene clusters displayed significant down-regulation across postnatal development and in adulthood (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 158,977 peaks with clear ATAC-seq signal compared with surrounding genomic regions were identified.
source: We identified 158,977 peaks with clear ATAC-seq signal compared with surrounding genomic regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the ATAC-seq peak calling analysis.

claim: Most accessible regions were located at distal intergenic regions (38%), introns (28%) and putative promoter regions (23%).
source: Most accessible regions were located at distal intergenic regions (38%), introns (28%) and putative promoter regions (23%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic annotation of ATAC-seq peaks shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Accessible regions encompassed sequences enriched for histone PTMs associated with active chromatin such as H3K4 mono-, di-, and tri-methylation.
source: and encompassed sequences enriched for histone PTMs associated with active chromatin such as H3K4 mono-, di-, and tri-methylation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of ATAC-seq data with ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Signal enrichment was higher for H3K4 methylation than for other histone PTMs.
source: Notably, signal enrichment was higher for H3K4 methylation than for other histone PTMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ChIP-seq signal analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ATAC-seq peaks are identified at regulatory elements such as enhancers and promoters and are preferentially located at genomic regions with nucleosomes carrying H3K4me.
source: These results are consistent with previous observations that ATAC-seq peaks are identified at regulatory elements such as enhancers and promoters and are preferentially located at genomic regions with nucleosomes carrying H3K4me (Henikoff et al., 2020; Bleckwehl et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on ATAC-seq.

claim: 3212 differentially accessible regions (DARs) were identified with a total of 760 regions with decreased chromatin accessibility (DARs-down) and 2452 regions with increased accessibility (DARs-up) in adult SPGs.
source: 3212 differentially accessible regions (DARs) were identified (adjusted-p ≤0.05, absLog2FC ≥1) with a total of 760 regions with decreased chromatin accessibility (DARs-down) and 2452 regions with increased accessibility (DARs-up) in adult SPGs (Figure 2A–B and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the differential accessibility analysis shown in Figure 2A–B.

claim: DARs were predominantly localized in distal intergenic regions (54% DARs-down, 37% DARs-up) and introns (33% DARs-down, 36% DARs-up) with a minority located in putative promoter regions (8% DARs-down, 12% DARs-up).
source: DARs were predominantly localized in distal intergenic regions (54% DARs-down, 37% DARs-up) and introns (33% DARs-down, 36% DARs-up) with a minority located in putative promoter regions (8% DARs-down, 12% DARs-up), consistent with the genomic distribution of all detected ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic annotation of DARs shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Genes closest to DARs are involved in male gonad development, cell adhesion, sex differentiation and regulation of cell communication among others.
source: GO analyses of the closest genes assigned to each DAR showed that these genes are involved in male gonad development, cell adhesion, sex differentiation and regulation of cell communication among others (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D–E.

claim: 51% of regions with increased accessibility are located at genomic loci that carry histone PTMs since early postnatal stages.
source: 51% of regions with increased accessibility are located at genomic loci that carry histone PTMs since early postnatal stages, and about half (48%) overlap with regions significantly enriched in H3K4me1, a histone PTM associated to enhancers.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of ATAC-seq data with ChIP-seq data for histone modifications.

claim: 48% of regions with increased accessibility overlap with regions significantly enriched in H3K4me1, a histone PTM associated to enhancers.
source: 51% of regions with increased accessibility are located at genomic loci that carry histone PTMs since early postnatal stages, and about half (48%) overlap with regions significantly enriched in H3K4me1, a histone PTM associated to enhancers.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of ATAC-seq data with ChIP-seq data for histone modifications.

claim: 80% of regions with decreased accessibility are located in regions with H3K4me1.
source: In contrast, 80% of regions with decreased accessibility are located in regions with H3K4me1 and 1/3 (33%) also overlap with the repressive histone PTM, H3K27me3 (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of ATAC-seq data with ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2F–G.

claim: 33% of regions with decreased accessibility also overlap with the repressive histone PTM, H3K27me3.
source: In contrast, 80% of regions with decreased accessibility are located in regions with H3K4me1 and 1/3 (33%) also overlap with the repressive histone PTM, H3K27me3 (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of ATAC-seq data with ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2F–G.

claim: 16% of regions with increased accessibility are located at potential active regulatory elements that carry H3K27ac.
source: Interestingly, while 16% of regions with increased accessibility are located at potential active regulatory elements that carry H3K27ac, none of the regions with decreased accessibility overlap with H3K27ac (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of ATAC-seq data with ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2F–G.

claim: None of the regions with decreased accessibility overlap with H3K27ac.
source: Interestingly, while 16% of regions with increased accessibility are located at potential active regulatory elements that carry H3K27ac, none of the regions with decreased accessibility overlap with H3K27ac (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of ATAC-seq data with ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2F–G.

claim: Regions with decreased accessibility in adult SPGs are enriched for binding motifs of members of specific TF families such as KLF, SP, FOXO, and ETS.
source: We observed that regions with decreased accessibility in adult SPGs are enriched for binding motifs of members of specific TF families such as KLF (KLF2, KLF5, KLF11, KLF12, KLF15, KLF16), SP (SP1-5, SP9), FOXO (FOXO1, FOXO3), ETS (ETV1-6) among others (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by TF motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Many TFs with enriched motifs in regions with decreased accessibility are differentially expressed in postnatal or adult SPGs (adjusted- p<0.05, 10 down-regulated and 11 up-regulated).
source: Expression analyses showed that many of these TFs are differentially expressed in postnatal or adult SPGs (adjusted- p<0.05, 10 down-regulated and 11 up-regulated; Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of motif analysis with RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B–C.

claim: KLF11, 12 and 15, TFs that regulate stem cell maintenance and development, are upregulated in adult SPGs compared to PND15.
source: For example, KLF11,12 and 15, TFs that regulate stem cell maintenance and development (Bialkowska et al., 2017), are upregulated in adult SPGs compared to PND15 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C and a citation to Bialkowska et al., 2017.

claim: SP5 has its lowest expression in adult SPGs.
source: SP5, which has its lowest expression in adult SPGs (Figure 3B–C), promotes self-renewal of mESCs by directly regulating Nanog (Tang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B–C.

claim: SP5 promotes self-renewal of mESCs by directly regulating Nanog.
source: SP5, which has its lowest expression in adult SPGs (Figure 3B–C), promotes self-renewal of mESCs by directly regulating Nanog (Tang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2017.

claim: FOXO3 has increased expression from PND15 onwards.
source: While FOXO3 has increased expression from PND15 onwards, FOXO1 is decreased in adult compared to postnatal SPGs (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B–C.

claim: FOXO1 is decreased in adult compared to postnatal SPGs.
source: While FOXO3 has increased expression from PND15 onwards, FOXO1 is decreased in adult compared to postnatal SPGs (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B–C.

claim: FOXO1 and FOXO3 regulate SSC function and maintenance in mouse.
source: Interestingly, FOXO1 and FOXO3 regulate SSC function and maintenance in mouse (Goertz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goertz et al., 2011.

claim: ELK4 is up-regulated in adult SPGs.
source: ELK4 is up-regulated in adult SPGs and can act as a transcriptional repressor via recruitment of the HDAC Sirt7 and deacetylation of H3K18ac (Figure 3B–C and E; Barber et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B–C and E.

claim: ELK4 can act as a transcriptional repressor via recruitment of the HDAC Sirt7 and deacetylation of H3K18ac.
source: ELK4 is up-regulated in adult SPGs and can act as a transcriptional repressor via recruitment of the HDAC Sirt7 and deacetylation of H3K18ac (Figure 3B–C and E; Barber et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barber et al., 2012.

claim: EKL4 can act as transcriptional activator of immediate early genes such as Fos.
source: EKL4 can also act as transcriptional activator of immediate early genes such as Fos (Dalton and Treisman, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dalton and Treisman, 1992.

claim: Fos codes for a TF important for the regulation of proliferation.
source: Interestingly, Fos itself codes for a TF important for the regulation of proliferation (He et al., 2008) and shows a trend towards up-regulation in adult SPGs (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to He et al., 2008.

claim: Fos shows a trend towards up-regulation in adult SPGs.
source: Interestingly, Fos itself codes for a TF important for the regulation of proliferation (He et al., 2008) and shows a trend towards up-regulation in adult SPGs (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: GABPA is downregulated in adult SPGs compared to PND15.
source: In contrast, GABPA is downregulated in adult SPGs compared to PND15 and has been involved in the regulation of proliferation in mESCs (Ueda et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and a citation to Ueda et al., 2017.

claim: GABPA has been involved in the regulation of proliferation in mESCs.
source: In contrast, GABPA is downregulated in adult SPGs compared to PND15 and has been involved in the regulation of proliferation in mESCs (Ueda et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ueda et al., 2017.

claim: Dmrt1 is progressively repressed during SPGs postnatal development and is the lowest in adult SPGs.
source: Dmrt1 is progressively repressed during SPGs postnatal development and is the lowest in adult SPGs (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B–D.

claim: DMRT1 can act either as a repressor or activator and controls testis development and male germ cell proliferation.
source: DMRT1 can act either as a repressor or activator and controls testis development and male germ cell proliferation (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: DMRT1 can inhibit meiosis and promote mitosis in SPGs by repressing Stra8.
source: DMRT1 can inhibit meiosis and promote mitosis in SPGs by repressing Stra8 (Matson et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Matson et al., 2010.

claim: Stra8 is transcriptionally repressed in adult SPGs.
source: Consistently, we observed transcriptional repression of Stra8 in adult SPGs (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Regions with increased chromatin accessibility in adult SPGs are enriched for binding motifs of members of specific TF families such as POU, RFX, DMRT, SOX, NFY, and AP-1.
source: The identified motifs correspond to binding motifs of members of specific TF families such as POU (POU2F2, POU1F1, POU5F1), RFX (RXF1-7), DMRT (DMRT1, DMRT3, DMRTA1-2, DMRTC2), SOX (SOX2, SOX3, SOX5, SOX13), NFY (NFYA, NFYB, NFYC), and AP-1 (JUN, JUNB, JUND, FOS, ATF3, BATF) (Figure 3F and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by TF motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A subset of TFs with motifs in regions with increased accessibility is differentially expressed (adjusted-p <0.05, 13 down-regulated and 5 up-regulated).
source: A subset of them is also differentially expressed (adjusted-p <0.05, 13 down-regulated and 5 up-regulated).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of motif analysis with RNA-seq data.

claim: The most overrepresented motif in regions with increased accessibility is similar to the binding motif of the POU family of TFs, which are critical regulators of stem cells.
source: The most overrepresented motif is similar to the binding motif of the POU family of TFs, which are critical regulators of stem cells (Nichols et al., 1998; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis and citations to studies on POU TFs.

claim: Pou1f1 and Pou5f1 are transcriptionally repressed in adult SPGs.
source: Pou1f1 and Pou5f1 are transcriptionally repressed in adult SPGs while Pou2f2 is maximally expressed in PND15 SPGs and down-regulated in adult cells (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3G–H.

claim: Pou2f2 is maximally expressed in PND15 SPGs and down-regulated in adult cells.
source: Pou1f1 and Pou5f1 are transcriptionally repressed in adult SPGs while Pou2f2 is maximally expressed in PND15 SPGs and down-regulated in adult cells (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3G–H.

claim: RFX family of TFs are master regulators of ciliogenesis.
source: We also identified motifs for members of the RFX family of TFs, which are master regulators of ciliogenesis (Choksi et al., 2014) implicated in regulation of neural stem cells (Kawase et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on RFX TFs.

claim: RFX2 is robustly expressed in adult SPGs.
source: RFX2 is robustly expressed in adult SPGs (Figure 3G–H and J)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3G–H and J.

claim: RFX2 has been reported to induce the expression of ciliary genes in association with the TF FOXJ.
source: and has been reported to induce the expression of ciliary genes in association with the TF FOXJ, which has a trend towards up-regulation in adult SPGs (Quigley and Kintner, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Quigley and Kintner, 2017.

claim: FOXJ has a trend towards up-regulation in adult SPGs.
source: and has been reported to induce the expression of ciliary genes in association with the TF FOXJ, which has a trend towards up-regulation in adult SPGs (Quigley and Kintner, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Ciliary genes are among the top genes specifically up-regulated in adult SPGs.
source: Interestingly, ciliary genes are among the top genes specifically up-regulated in adult SPGs (Figure 1H), suggesting a regulatory relationship between RFX2 and ciliary genes expression in adult SPG cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: There is a regulatory relationship between RFX2 and ciliary genes expression in adult SPG cells.
source: Interestingly, ciliary genes are among the top genes specifically up-regulated in adult SPGs (Figure 1H), suggesting a regulatory relationship between RFX2 and ciliary genes expression in adult SPG cells.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the co-occurrence of RFX2 expression and ciliary gene upregulation.

claim: In mESCs, NF-Y TFs facilitate a permissive chromatin conformation and play an important role in the expression of core ESC pluripotency genes.
source: In mESCs, NF-Y TFs facilitate a permissive chromatin conformation and play an important role in the expression of core ESC pluripotency genes (Oldfield et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oldfield et al., 2014.

claim: NF-YA/B motif enrichment has been found in regions of open chromatin in human SPGs.
source: NF-YA/B motif enrichment has also been found in regions of open chromatin in human SPGs (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2017.

claim: The expression of NF-YA and NF-YC is progressively down-regulated starting at PND15.
source: Interestingly, the expression of NF-YA and NF-YC is progressively down-regulated starting at PND15 (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3G–H.

claim: AP-1 family of TFs are involved in many processes, from regulation of cell proliferation to differentiation and acute responses to environmental clues.
source: We also detected an enrichment for the binding motifs of members of the AP-1 family of TFs, which are involved in many processes, from regulation of cell proliferation to differentiation and acute responses to environmental clues (Bejjani et al., 2019; Vierbuchen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on AP-1 TFs.

claim: Except for Fosl2, other AP-1 TFs do not show any significant change in transcription in postnatal or adult SPGs and are either constitutively expressed or repressed.
source: Interestingly, except for Fosl2, other TFs do not show any significant change in transcription in postnatal or adult SPGs and are either constitutively expressed or repressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Fos and JUN are robustly expressed in postnatal and adult SPGs.
source: For instance, Fos and JUN are robustly expressed in postnatal and adult SPGs (Figure 3I) consistent with their role in promoting the proliferative potential of SSCs (He et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Fos and JUN have a role in promoting the proliferative potential of SSCs.
source: For instance, Fos and JUN are robustly expressed in postnatal and adult SPGs (Figure 3I) consistent with their role in promoting the proliferative potential of SSCs (He et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to He et al., 2008 and Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Down-regulated genes in adult SPGs had no significant difference in chromatin accessibility at promoter regions, despite a trend for decreased accessibility around the TSS.
source: No significant difference was detected for down-regulated genes in adult SPGs, despite a trend for decreased accessibility around the TSS (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of ATAC-seq signal at promoters shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Down-regulated genes in adult SPGs had a significant increase in chromatin accessibility in their gene body.
source: However, down-regulated genes had a significant increase in chromatin accessibility in their body (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Up-regulated genes in adult SPGs had a significant increase in chromatin accessibility both at the promoter region and gene body.
source: Up-regulated genes had a significant increase in chromatin accessibility both at the promoter region and gene body (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: Binding motifs for members of KLF and SP family of TFs were overrepresented in the promoter of both down- and up-regulated DEGs.
source: Binding motifs for members of KLF and SP family of TFs were overrepresented in the promoter of both down- and up-regulated DEGs, while motifs for members of TF families SOX and NFY were detected only in the promoter of down-regulated genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis at promoters of DEGs.

claim: Motifs for members of TF families SOX and NFY were detected only in the promoter of down-regulated genes.
source: Binding motifs for members of KLF and SP family of TFs were overrepresented in the promoter of both down- and up-regulated DEGs, while motifs for members of TF families SOX and NFY were detected only in the promoter of down-regulated genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis at promoters of DEGs.

claim: Promoters of up-regulated genes were specifically enriched in motifs for RFX and AP-1.
source: Promoters of up-regulated genes were specifically enriched in motifs for RFX and AP-1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Changes in chromatin accessibility at the promoter of up-regulated DEGs may be associated with differential binding of RFX and AP-1 TFs.
source: These observations suggest that changes in chromatin accessibility, in particular at the promoter of up-regulated DEGs may be associated with differential binding of RFX and AP-1 TFs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the co-occurrence of motif enrichment and chromatin accessibility changes.

claim: Only 3.2% of all promoters of DEGs overlap with at least one DAR.
source: Unexpectedly, only 3.2% of all promoters of DEGs overlap with at least one DAR (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The majority of overlapping DARs (71%) is associated with promoters of up-regulated genes in adult SPGs.
source: The majority of overlapping DARs (71%) is associated with promoters of up-regulated genes in adult SPGs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Gpx4, a peroxidase involved in the control of stemness, is transcriptionally active in adult SPGs and has an open chromatin at its promoter region.
source: For example, Gpx4, a peroxidase involved in the control of stemness (Hu et al., 2021), is transcriptionally active in adult SPGs and has an open chromatin at its promoter region (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4E and a citation to Hu et al., 2021.

claim: A third of DEGs were associated with at least one DAR within +/-100 kb.
source: We observed that a third of DEGs were associated with at least one DAR (Figure 4F)
evidence: This claim is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The majority of DARs (69%) within +/-100 kb of DEGs overlap regulatory elements of up-regulated genes.
source: with the majority of DARs (69%) overlapping regulatory elements of up-regulated genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the overlap analysis.

claim: Braf is transcriptionally up-regulated in adult SPGs, which correlates with increased chromatin accessibility at distal regulatory elements.
source: For instance, Braf is transcriptionally up-regulated in adult SPGs, which correlates with increased chromatin accessibility at distal regulatory elements (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Only a fraction of DEGs is associated with DARs, suggesting that changes in gene expression are not always mirrored at the level of chromatin accessibility.
source: Our results overall show that only a fraction of DEGs is associated with DARs, suggesting that changes in gene expression are not always mirrored at the level of chromatin accessibility, consistent with recent observations (Kiani et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis and supported by a citation to Kiani et al., 2022.

claim: TEs are tightly regulated in the germline by coordinated epigenetic mechanisms involving DNA methylation, chromatin silencing and PIWI proteins-piRNA pathway.
source: TEs are tightly regulated in the germline by coordinated epigenetic mechanisms involving DNA methylation, chromatin silencing and PIWI proteins-piRNA pathway (Deniz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Deniz et al., 2019.

claim: SPGs have a unique landscape of chromatin accessibility at long-terminal repeats (LTRs) retrotransposons, compared with other stages of germ cells in testis.
source: SPGs were recently shown to have a unique landscape of chromatin accessibility at long-terminal repeats (LTRs) retrotransposons, compared with other stages of germ cells in testis (Sakashita et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sakashita et al., 2020.

claim: SPGs transitioning from PND15 to adult stages have significantly different chromatin accessibility at 135 TEs subtypes.
source: These analyses showed that SPGs transitioning from PND15 to adult stages have significantly different chromatin accessibility at 135 TEs subtypes (adjusted-p ≤0.05, absLog2FC ≥1) (Figure 5A–B and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential accessibility analysis of TEs shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: Most TEs subtypes have decreased chromatin accessibility (93/135, 68.9%) in adult SPGs.
source: Most TEs subtypes have decreased chromatin accessibility (93/135, 68,9%) (Figure 5A) and 42 have increased accessibility (Figure 5B) in adult SPGs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential accessibility analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 42 TEs subtypes have increased accessibility in adult SPGs.
source: Most TEs subtypes have decreased chromatin accessibility (93/135, 68,9%) (Figure 5A) and 42 have increased accessibility (Figure 5B) in adult SPGs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential accessibility analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Differentially accessible TEs loci are predominantly located in intergenic (68%) and intronic (25%) regions and 6% are close to a gene (+/-1 kb from TSS).
source: Differentially accessible TEs loci are predominantly located in intergenic (68%) and intronic (25%) regions and 6% re close to a gene (+/-1 kb from TSS; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic annotation shown in Figure 5C.

claim: LTR retrotransposons were the most abundant TEs with altered chromatin accessibility, specifically ERVK and ERV1 subtypes.
source: LTR retrotransposons were the most abundant TEs with altered chromatin accessibility, specifically ERVK and ERV1 subtypes (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: Enrichment of RLTR17 and RLTR9 repeats was previously reported in mESCs, specifically at TFs important for pluripotency maintenance such as Pou5f1 and Nanog.
source: Enrichment of RLTR17 and RLTR9 repeats was previously reported in mESCs, specifically at TFs important for pluripotency maintenance such as Pou5f1 and Nanog (Fort et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fort et al., 2014.

claim: The promoter region of the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) Lncenc1 harbors several LTR loci with decreased accessibility in adult SPGs.
source: Interestingly, we identified the promoter region of the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) Lncenc1, an important regulator of pluripotency in mESCs (Fort et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018), to harbor several LTR loci with decreased accessibility in adult SPGs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the ATAC-seq data analysis.

claim: Lncenc1 is an important regulator of pluripotency in mESCs.
source: Interestingly, we identified the promoter region of the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) Lncenc1, an important regulator of pluripotency in mESCs (Fort et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018), to harbor several LTR loci with decreased accessibility in adult SPGs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fort et al., 2014 and Sun et al., 2018.

claim: RLTR17 overlaps with the TSS of Lncenc1, and its decreased accessibility correlates with markedly lower Lncenc1 expression in adult SPGs.
source: One of these loci, RLTR17, overlaps with the TSS of Lncenc1, and its decreased accessibility correlates with markedly lower Lncenc1 expression in adult SPGs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrated analysis of ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Lncenc1 (also known as Platr18) is part of the pluripotency-associated transcript (Platr) family of lncRNAs identified as potential regulators of pluripotency-associated genes Pou5f1, Nanog and Zfp42 in mESCs.
source: Lncenc1 (also known as Platr18) is part of the pluripotency-associated transcript (Platr) family of lncRNAs identified as potential regulators of pluripotency-associated genes Pou5f1, Nanog and Zfp42 in mESCs (Bergmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bergmann et al., 2015.

claim: Platr27 and Platr14 have TSS that overlap with LTRs with reduced accessibility, RLTR17 and RLTR16B_MM, respectively.
source: We identified several other Platr genes such as Platr27 and Platr14, whose TSS overlaps with LTRs with reduced accessibility, RLTR17 and RLTR16B_MM, respectively (Figure 5D and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Platr27 and Platr14 tended to be downregulated in adult SPGs but were unchanged at PND8 and PND15.
source: These two pluripotency-associated transcripts tended to be downregulated in adult SPGs but were unchanged at PND8 and PND15 (Figure 5D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Many LINE L1 subtypes had increased chromatin accessibility in adult SPGs.
source: Interestingly, many LINE L1 subtypes had increased chromatin accessibility in adult SPGs (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential accessibility analysis of TEs.

claim: Several L1 loci are situated less than +/-5 kb from the TSS of olfactory (Olfr) genes, particularly Olfr gene clusters on chromosome 2, 7, and 11.
source: When parsing the data for more accessible loci within L1 subtypes, we found several L1 loci situated less than +/-5 kb from the TSS of olfactory (Olfr) genes, particularly Olfr gene clusters on chromosome 2, 7, and 11 (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic annotation of differentially accessible L1 loci.

claim: TEs provide tissue-specific substrates for TF binding.
source: TEs are known to provide tissue-specific substrates for TF binding (Sundaram and Wysocka, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sundaram and Wysocka, 2020.

claim: Among LTR families with less accessible chromatin, ERVKs had the highest number of enriched TF motifs in adult SPGs.
source: We grouped LTR subtypes by family (EVK, ERV1, ERVL and ERVL-MaLR families) and observed that among families with less accessible chromatin, ERVKs had the highest number of enriched TF motifs in adult SPGs (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of differentially accessible LTRs.

claim: More accessible LINE L1 subtypes were highly enriched in TF motifs, particularly in multiple members of ETS, E2F and FOX families.
source: More accessible LINE L1 subtypes were highly enriched in TF motifs, particularly in multiple members of ETS, E2F and FOX families (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of differentially accessible LINE L1 elements.

claim: The most significant motifs in more accessible LINE L1 subtypes belonged to SSCs maintenance and stem cell potential regulators FOXO1 and ZEB1.
source: The most significant motifs belonged to SSCs maintenance and stem cell potential regulators FOXO1 and ZEB1, as well as TFs recently associated with active enhancers of the stem-cell-enriched population of SPGs such as ZBTB17 and KLF5 (Supplementary file 5; Cheng et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis and a citation to Cheng et al., 2020.

claim: Postnatal maturation of SPGs is accompanied by an overall decrease in the expression of pluripotency markers and differential expression of signaling molecules and regulators of cell cycle and spermatogenesis.
source: The present data complement previous findings by showing that postnatal maturation of SPGs is accompanied by an overall decrease in the expression of pluripotency markers and differential expression of signaling molecules and regulators of cell cycle and spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The transition from early to mid-postnatal stage (PND8 to PND15) is accompanied by changes in gene expression.
source: For instance, we observed that while the transition from early to mid-postnatal stage (PND8 to PND15) is accompanied by changes in gene expression, the transition from mid-postnatal to adult stage is more extensive, both in number of regulated genes and magnitude of changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression analysis.

claim: The transition from mid-postnatal to adult stage is more extensive than PND8 to PND15, both in number of regulated genes and magnitude of changes.
source: For instance, we observed that while the transition from early to mid-postnatal stage (PND8 to PND15) is accompanied by changes in gene expression, the transition from mid-postnatal to adult stage is more extensive, both in number of regulated genes and magnitude of changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression analysis showing more DEGs between PND15 and adult.

claim: There is a clear trend towards up-regulation of gene expression as postnatal maturation proceeds.
source: We also observed a clear trend towards up-regulation of gene expression as postnatal maturation proceeds, that may reflect gradual transcriptional increase for some genes and possibly sharp changes at certain developmental stages for others.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of more up-regulated than down-regulated genes.

claim: Several transcriptional repressors and epigenetic silencers are differentially down-regulated which may explain the marked trend towards transcriptional up-regulation.
source: Notably, several transcriptional repressors and epigenetic silencers are differentially down-regulated which may explain the marked trend towards transcriptional up-regulation in our datasets (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed downregulation of repressors and the overall trend of upregulation.

claim: A global down-regulation of histone genes starting at PND15 may modify the composition and structure of chromatin and be associated with chromatin openness.
source: Interestingly, we also observed a global down-regulation of histone genes starting at PND15 (Supplementary file 1), which may modify the composition and structure of chromatin and be associated with chromatin openness (Prado et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed downregulation of histone genes and a citation to Prado et al., 2017.

claim: The transition of SPGs from early postnatal to adult stage is accompanied by changes in chromatin accessibility, in particular, increased accessibility at enhancer regions in adult compared to postnatal SPGs.
source: Our results suggest that the transition of SPGs from early postnatal to adult stage is accompanied by changes in chromatin accessibility. In particular, accessibility is increased in regions enriched in H3K4me1, a histone PTM typically associated with primed enhancers, but also to a lesser extent, in regions enriched in H3K27ac, a mark associated with active regulatory elements (Gasperini et al., 2020; Shlyueva et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the ATAC-seq data analysis and integration with ChIP-seq data.

claim: Enhancer priming has recently been proposed as an important mechanism for SPGs differentiation.
source: Enhancer priming has recently been proposed as an important mechanism for SPGs differentiation (McCarrey, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McCarrey, 2023.

claim: Differences in chromatin accessibility may be partially explained by differential binding of TFs to regulatory elements.
source: Differences in chromatin accessibility may be partially explained by differential binding of TFs to regulatory elements (Klemm et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Klemm et al., 2019.

claim: CpG methylation and nucleosome positioning can influence TF binding at regulatory elements and affect chromatin accessibility.
source: For instance, CpG methylation and nucleosome positioning can influence TF binding at regulatory elements and affect chromatin accessibility (Barisic et al., 2019; Kaluscha et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barisic et al., 2019 and Kaluscha et al., 2022.

claim: The fact that Dnmt1 is downregulated in adult SPGs concomitantly with differential expression of TFs and chromatin modifiers may explain changes in chromatin accessibility at potential enhancers.
source: The fact that Dnmt1 is downregulated in adult SPGs concomitantly with differential expression of TFs and chromatin modifiers may explain changes in chromatin accessibility at potential enhancers.
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting the downregulation of Dnmt1 with chromatin accessibility changes.

claim: Transcriptional regulation and chromatin accessibility at regulatory elements are not always linked and can be dissociated.
source: This suggests that transcriptional regulation and chromatin accessibility at regulatory elements are not always linked and can be dissociated, as previously reported (Chereji et al., 2019; Kiani et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by citations to Chereji et al., 2019 and Kiani et al., 2022.

claim: Chromatin accessibility may be modified without any effects on transcription and conversely, transcription can be activated or repressed without requiring any change in chromatin accessibility.
source: This implies that chromatin accessibility may be modified without any effects on transcription and conversely, transcription can be activated or repressed without requiring any change in chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed lack of correspondence between transcription and accessibility.

claim: Changes in chromatin accessibility may have no immediate effects on transcription but reflect an intermediate state that primes a gene or genomic locus for later activation or repression.
source: It is also possible that changes in chromatin accessibility have no immediate effects on transcription but reflect an intermediate state that primes a gene or genomic locus for later activation or repression such as observed with developmentally- or experience-dependent primed enhancers (Marco et al., 2020; Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to Marco et al., 2020 and Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011.

claim: The majority of DARs with increased accessibility overlap with regions enriched in H3K4me1, a histone modification characteristic of primed enhancers.
source: Consistently, the majority of DARs with increased accessibility overlap with regions enriched in H3K4me1, a histone modification characteristic of primed enhancers thought to control future transcriptional responses in different cell types (Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data and a citation to Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011.

claim: Primed enhancers are thought to control future transcriptional responses in different cell types.
source: Consistently, the majority of DARs with increased accessibility overlap with regions enriched in H3K4me1, a histone modification characteristic of primed enhancers thought to control future transcriptional responses in different cell types (Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011.

claim: Regions with increased accessibility may be important for responses to external cues in adult SPGs.
source: These regions may be important for responses to external cues in adult SPGs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential function of regions with increased accessibility.

claim: Chromatin accessibility has been suggested to not necessarily be the primary determinant of chromatin-mediated gene regulation.
source: Chromatin accessibility has been suggested to not necessarily be the primary determinant of chromatin-mediated gene regulation (Chereji et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chereji et al., 2019.

claim: ERVK and ERV1 subtypes are known to play an important role in the regulation of mRNA and lncRNAs transcription during spermatogenesis.
source: Notably, ERVKs are known to play an important role in the regulation of mRNA and lncRNAs transcription during spermatogenesis (Davis et al., 2017; Sakashita et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Davis et al., 2017 and Sakashita et al., 2020.

claim: The landscape of chromatin accessibility at LTRs loci in SPGs is unique compared to other mitotic germ cells and meiotic gametes in testis.
source: The landscape of chromatin accessibility at LTRs loci in SPGs is known to be unique compared to other mitotic germ cells and meiotic gametes in testis (Sakashita et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sakashita et al., 2020.

claim: RLTR17 has been shown to provide binding sites for the pluripotency factors Oct4 and Nanog in mESCs.
source: In mESCs, it is highly expressed and enriched in open chromatin regions and has been shown to provide binding sites for the pluripotency factors Oct4 and Nanog (Fort et al., 2014; Xiong et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fort et al., 2014 and Xiong et al., 2022.

claim: RLTR17 chromatin organization may play a role in regulating pluripotency programs between early postnatal and adult SPGs.
source: Therefore, we suggest that RLTR17 chromatin organization may play a role in regulating pluripotency programs between early postnatal and adult SPGs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed changes in RLTR17 accessibility and its known role in pluripotency.

claim: Recent findings in mouse and human ESCs suggest a non-random genomic localization of L1 elements, specifically at genes encoding proteins with specialized functions.
source: Recent findings in mouse and human ESCs suggest a non-random genomic localization of L1 elements, specifically at genes encoding proteins with specialized functions (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2020.

claim: The Olfr gene family was the most enriched in L1 elements.
source: Among them, the Olfr gene family was the most enriched in L1 elements (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2020.

claim: Olfr proteins have been implicated in swimming behaviour of sperm cells.
source: Although their role in SPGs is currently not established, Olfr proteins have been implicated in swimming behaviour of sperm cells (Fukuda and Touhara, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fukuda and Touhara, 2006.

claim: Olfr genes may play additional roles in spermatogenesis, other than in sperm physiology.
source: Given their dynamic regulation in SPGs, we speculate that Olfr genes play additional roles in spermatogenesis, other than in sperm physiology.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed changes in Olfr gene expression and L1 accessibility.

claim: The study reveals an age-dependent dynamic reorganization of chromatin accessibility in SPGs.
source: Nevertheless, by comparing chromatin landscape in developing and adult SPGs, the study reveals an age-dependent dynamic reorganization of chromatin accessibility in these cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the ATAC-seq data analysis.

claim: The data provide novel insight into transcriptome-chromatin dynamics of mouse SPGs from early postnatal life to adulthood with great depth and high resolution.
source: When integrated with our transcriptomic datasets and published histone PTMs profiles, the data provide novel insight into transcriptome-chromatin dynamics of mouse SPGs from early postnatal life to adulthood with great depth and high resolution.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the study.
